title: The pull home
hook: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, homesick for his bride

segments.voice: Yesterday: the king and queen on the rooftop, and your line, everyone loves themselves. Did you spare someone a slight? Today, a monk who can't stop thinking about home. Day six hundred seventeen.

First semester away. The new place is supposed to be the start of everything, and all you can think about is the kitchen at home, the dog, someone's voice saying come back soon. Nanda knew that feeling. He was the Buddha's half-brother, the son of Mahapajapati, and he had become a monk. But one day he tells the other monks: I'm not happy living this life. I can't keep it up. I'm going to give up the training and go back. Why? Because of a girl. Today: the pull home.
screen: `FIRST SEMESTER AWAY.` → `NANDA, THE HALF-BROTHER.` → `I CAN'T KEEP IT UP.`

segments.voice: When I left home, Nanda tells the Buddha, a Sakyan girl, the loveliest in the land, looked up at me with her hair half combed and said: come back soon, master. I keep remembering it. What the Buddha does next is the strangest part of the story. He takes Nanda by the arm and, the text says, as easily as a strong man bends his arm, the two vanish and appear in the heaven of the Thirty-Three. There Nanda sees five hundred heavenly nymphs. Which is lovelier, the Buddha asks, the Sakyan girl or these? Next to these, Nanda says, she's nothing at all. Then practice, the Buddha says, and I promise you these. So Nanda practices. But the other monks hear about the deal and start teasing him: Nanda the hired hand, Nanda working for wages. Ashamed, Nanda goes off alone and practices in earnest. And somewhere in that practice, the wanting itself falls away, both the girl and the nymphs. He goes back to the Buddha and says: I release you from your promise. I already knew, the Buddha says. The verse praises one who has crossed the mud of sense-desire and is no longer shaken by pleasure or pain. Many teachers read it as a bigger desire used to loosen a smaller one, until both drop away. And the ending is plain in the text: the pull wasn't beaten by force. It simply stopped pulling.
screen: `COME BACK SOON, MASTER.` · `THE HEAVEN OF THE THIRTY-THREE.` · `NANDA THE HIRED HAND.` · `I RELEASE YOU FROM YOUR PROMISE.` · then, large: `THE PULL HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice what pulls you back. Sit and settle. Ask, gently: what tugs at me when I try to keep a good intention? A habit, a person, a comfort, a picture in my head? Let it come, the way Nanda's memory came, the half-combed hair, the voice. Don't fight it and don't follow it. Just feel the pull in the body, where it lives. Then rest with the breath, and notice that the pull, too, rises and fades. The bell holds the time.
The pull home. Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, homesick for the girl he left, until the wanting itself fell away. Today's word.
Your line: the pull home. Today, when an old habit tugs at you, name it, feel it, and watch how long it lasts if you don't follow it. Day six hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Nanda's story is often told in Buddhist communities, and in the Anguttara Nikaya Nanda is named foremost among monks in guarding the senses, the discipline he came to after his struggle.

fork.setup: you're Nanda. the other monks are mocking you for practicing just to win heavenly nymphs. what do you do?
options: leave the order and go home.
go off alone and practice in earnest.
fork.reveal: ashamed, he withdraws and practices seriously, and reaches the end of craving. then he releases the Buddha from the promise.

original.note: Pali Nanda: a name meaning joy or delight.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha bribed his brother with heaven.
what it means: one desire was used to loosen another, until in real practice both fell away and the promise was released.
what a scholar hears: Udana 3.2 is the source for Nanda's story, retold at length in Ashvaghosha's Sanskrit poem Saundarananda; AN 1 names Nanda foremost in guarding the senses.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadagga Vagga (Nanda foremost in guarding the senses)

notes: Udana 3.2 paraphrased. The text's comparison (the Sakyan girl next to the nymphs is like a mutilated she-monkey) is softened to 'she's nothing at all'; confirm.
The text calls the nymphs 'dove-footed'; the number five hundred is the text's.
Confirm AN 1 etadagga for Nanda (indriyesu guttadvara) and the reference to Ashvaghosha's Saundarananda.
The 'teachers have read the story in different ways' framing is the writer's; a Keeper may want to name a traditional reading.
